title: Action, never the fruit
hookLine: Arjuna won't fight, and Krishna answers with two plain words, action and fruit: the heart of karma yoga
carry: karma yoga: the work is yours, the fruit isn't
tomorrow: you ask to be led. from where, to where?
last: TEACH ME. I WILL NOT FIGHT.

cards: Arjuna has laid down his bow, because every result he can picture is terrible. Krishna doesn't promise him the results will be fine. He says something stranger, in one of the most quoted lines in the Gita.
Two plain core words sit in it, karma and phala, and readers inside the tradition still hear it two ways.

teach.b: Here's the half line: karmany evadhikaras te ma phaleshu kadachana. Karma: action, a deed; here karmani, in action. Phala: fruit, the result a deed brings; here phaleshu, in the fruits.
Kadachana, ever, closes it like a door.
Krishna, to Arjuna: your claim is in action alone, never in its fruits. The verse goes on: don't let the fruit be your motive, and don't cling to not acting either. So, do results matter at all?
One reading: let go of the fruit entirely. Work done for a reward binds; work done as an offering frees. Later in the Gita, Krishna asks that whatever is done be offered to him.
The other reading: the verse never says don't care how it turns out.

teach.h: LET THE FRUIT GO, OR IT ISN'T OWED.
teach.b: It says the fruit isn't owed to you. You still aim, still give it everything, since the same verse rules out slacking off. What you drop is the demand.
Neither reading says the work doesn't matter.
And together they name one of the Gita's great paths: karma yoga, the yoga of action. Do your dharma, your rightful work, fully, offer it, and loosen your grip on what it brings.

teach.h: THE WORK IS YOURS. THE FRUIT ISN'T.
teach.b: That's why many Hindus begin a day's work or an exam with a short prayer, offering the work itself. For Arjuna, it means: pick up the bow, and stop bargaining with the outcome.

how: Hindus often recite Gita 2.47 as a reminder of karma yoga, acting without clinging to results, and many begin work or an exam with a short prayer offering the work; teachers in different schools explain the verse differently.

o: the Gita's path of action without clinging

games.q: the line, word by word — tap the pairs.

s: karma in this verse means what goes around comes around
here it's the plain word for action, set beside phala, fruit. the law of karma is a real teaching too, but this line is about doing.
the same verse warns against clinging to not acting
the claim is to action, and inaction isn't the way out.
karma yoga means doing your work as an offering, without clinging to its fruit
the Gita names it a path: karma yoga, the yoga of action.

games.q: a friend reads Gita 2.47 as 'just don't care how it turns out.' give her the other reading's best case.
o: you still aim and work fully; you just don't treat the result as owed to you.
results don't really exist, so how you work makes no difference.
only the result counts, so the verse is about winning calmly.
games.why: the steelman: the fruit isn't your claim, but the same verse rules out slacking. what's dropped is the demand, not the effort.

practice: Pick one thing you're working toward this week. Silently name the result you're hoping for, then the one action that's actually yours to do today.
Hold the action, and set the hoped-for result down beside you like a bag at your feet. If you pray, offer the action, the way Krishna asks: whatever you do, do it as an offering.
If you don't, simply say: the work is mine; the result isn't owed. Breathe.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words: plain ones that keep coming back. Today, karma, action, and phala, the fruit it bears: two words the Gita sets apart on purpose.

orig.note: Sanskrit: your claim is in action alone (Bhagavad Gita 2.47).

carryVoice: One to keep: karma yoga. The work is yours; the fruit isn't. Arjuna, pick up the bow. Rest easy.
